generatedProse.concept-context: Across the School of Sport, a placement or applied project offers what no lecture or seminar can: contact with real athletes, real data and real decisions. A few weeks in a performance lab, a coaching setting, a sports clinic or a development project can build practical skills, strengthen your employability for competitive routes, and show you which part of the field actually suits you. The settings differ by subject, a physiology lab for a sport science student, a club for a coaching student, a clinic for a therapy student, but the gain comes most fully to the student who arrives knowing what they want from the time.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Two sport and exercise science students take up the same month-long placement in a performance physiology lab.

Tom turns up each day, runs the fitness tests he is given, and goes home. The data gets collected. But Tom never decided what the placement was for, so it drifts: no goal to steer by, no sense of what to notice about how testing is run, nothing gathered beyond the hours logged. At the end there is little to show but attendance.

Amara starts the same placement with two or three clear aims: to learn how the lab calibrates and runs a VO2 max test, to understand how athlete data is handled and reported, and to leave with examples for a sport science graduate application. Those aims shape each day, what to volunteer for, what to ask the physiologists, what to note. The same month yields skills, insight and evidence.

Both served the same time. Only Amara decided in advance what to draw from it, and so actually drew it.
generatedProse.summary: A placement in the School of Sport offers real skills, employability and self-knowledge, but only to the student who aims for them. You can now identify what such an experience can give you, recognise the difference between drifting and drawing value, and set clear aims of your own. The next lesson turns those aims into action: the moves that get the most out of the experience while you are in it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made Amara's month in the physiology lab more valuable than Tom's?

items.text: She set clear aims in advance, which shaped what she did, asked and gathered.
She was given more interesting tests than Tom was.
She spent more hours in the lab than Tom did.
She was naturally more confident than Tom.

feedback.correct: That's right. Amara set aims in advance, and those aims steered what she did, asked and gathered across the month.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what Amara decided before the placement began.
feedback.incorrectFinal: Amara's month was more valuable because she set clear aims in advance, which steered the whole placement, not because of better tests, more hours or confidence.
